opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me most is that we're at a point where AI has gone from being a research artifact to being a real component in production systems, but the way we build with it still feels a bit like the early days of programming, before we had good abstractions, testing practices, or debugging tools.

If you look at the history of computer science, a lot of progress came from taking something messy and unreliable and building layers around it that make it dependable. Distributed systems are a good example. Individual machines fail all the time, networks are unreliable, yet we learned to build systems on top that are highly available and correct. I think we're facing a similar challenge with large language models. They're incredibly powerful, but they're also non-deterministic, they hallucinate, and their behavior can shift when you change a prompt slightly or swap in a new model version.

So the question becomes: how do you engineer reliable systems out of unreliable components? That's where software engineering techniques come in. Things like modularity, being able to break a complex AI application into smaller pieces you can reason about and test independently. Things like specification, actually writing down what you expect the system to do so you can check it. Evaluation and testing, which for AI is much harder because outputs aren't simply right or wrong in a binary way. And debugging and observability, so when something goes wrong in a multi-step agent pipeline, you can actually trace where it went wrong and why.

What I find exciting is that many of these problems are still wide open. There's a lot of room for new ideas, new systems, and new tools. And historically, when you solve these kinds of infrastructure problems, you unlock a huge wave of applications, because suddenly many more developers can build things they trust. I think we're right at the beginning of that for AI, and it's a very fun place to be as a researcher and as a builder.

r001.rationale: The response describes building dependable systems from non-deterministic AI components, but it does not clearly identify making AI systems more predictable as an exciting outcome.

r002.rationale: It identifies specification, evaluation, and testing as ways to check AI systems against expected behavior.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies debugging and observability as ways to trace where a multi-step AI pipeline failed and why.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. What excites me most is that we're finally at a point where we can stop treating AI as a kind of magic and start treating it as a systems problem, which is what it actually is.

I've spent most of my career building distributed systems, from Spark to Ray, and the lesson that keeps coming back is that the hard part is rarely the core algorithm. The hard part is everything around it: reliability, scaling, debugging, composing pieces that were never designed to work together. Large language models are no different. A single model call is impressive, but a real application is a pipeline of calls, retrievals, tool invocations, and verification steps, and today those pipelines are brittle. They fail silently, they're expensive, and nobody can tell you why a given answer came out the way it did.

Software engineering has decades of answers to exactly those problems. We know how to do testing, versioning, observability, fault tolerance, separation of concerns. The exciting thing is that most of those ideas have barely been applied to AI systems yet. So there's enormous low-hanging fruit.

Let me give a concrete example. When we were building Ray, the question was how you make a Python programmer productive on a cluster without them having to think about scheduling or failures. The analogous question now is how you make a developer productive building with models that are nondeterministic, slow, and occasionally wrong. That's a compiler problem, a runtime problem, and an evaluation problem all at once. Projects like vLLM on the serving side, or Chatbot Arena on the evaluation side, are really about bringing rigor to parts of the stack that were previously ad hoc.

The other thing I find energizing is that the feedback loop goes both ways. We're using software engineering to make AI more dependable, but AI is also starting to change how we write software. Once the models can reason about systems, we can hand them the boring parts of the work, and then the engineering question becomes how do you verify what they produce. I think the next few years will be defined by that interplay, and that's a very good time to be a systems person.

r001.rationale: The response describes improving reliability and dependability, but does not clearly identify making AI systems more predictable.

r002.rationale: It presents verification as part of building AI applications and says engineers must verify what models produce.

r003.rationale: It names debugging among the software engineering practices that can be applied to AI systems.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is making AI systems easier to build, understand, and improve. With software, we have developed practices around testing, debugging, modularity, and monitoring. AI needs that same discipline, but it also introduces a challenge: the behavior is probabilistic. A change can improve one task and make another worse.

So the opportunity is to build a much better feedback loop. Can you measure whether a change actually helps? Can you trace a failure to the model, the data, or another component? Can you improve quality while reducing latency and cost? Making those questions easier to answer would let developers spend less time guessing and more time building useful applications.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI behavior as probabilistic and proposes measuring changes, but it does not clearly identify making systems more predictable as an exciting application.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes measuring whether a change helps, which clearly communicates verifying the effects of changes to AI systems.

r003.rationale: It names debugging and describes tracing failures to the model, data, or another component.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is making AI systems easier to build, more reliable, and accessible to more people. A model is a very important component, but it’s only one component of an application. You also have data, infrastructure, monitoring, and feedback from users, and all of these have to work together.

Software engineering gives us a way to manage that complexity: modularity, clear interfaces, testing, and tools that help developers iterate quickly. The interesting challenge is adapting those techniques to systems whose behavior is probabilistic. How do you test an application when there isn’t always one correct answer? How do you detect that a change improved one capability but hurt another?

If we can make that development cycle more systematic, a small team can build something useful without having to become experts in every layer of the stack. That’s the part I find particularly exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says software engineering can make AI systems more reliable, but it does not clearly identify making them more predictable.

r002.rationale: It describes testing systems and detecting whether changes improve or harm capabilities, communicating a way to verify their behavior.

r003.rationale: The response discusses testing and monitoring, but does not identify enabling developers to debug AI systems.
